```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Helper for kable tables and LaTeX export
ftab <- function(x, digits = 3, caption = NULL, latex_file = NULL, row.names = NULL, ...) {
    if (is.null(row.names)) {
        row.names <- !is.data.frame(x)
    }
    if (!is.null(latex_file)) {
        dir.create("../output/tables_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
        filepath <- file.path("../output/tables_q", paste0(latex_file, ".tex"))

        # Clean caption for LaTeX
        clean_caption <- caption
        if (!is.null(clean_caption)) {
            clean_caption <- gsub("\u03b2", "$\\\\beta$", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("\u03b1", "$\\\\alpha$", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("\u2192", "$\\\\rightarrow$", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("\u2014", "---", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub(" \u2014 ", " --- ", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("≤", "$\\\\le$", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("ρ", "$\\\\rho$", clean_caption)
            clean_caption <- gsub("%", "\\\\%", clean_caption)
        }

        # Generate LaTeX table code
        latex_code <- knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, caption = clean_caption, booktabs = TRUE, format = "latex", row.names = row.names, ...)
        writeLines(as.character(latex_code), filepath)
    }
    knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, caption = caption, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = row.names, ...) |>
        kable_styling(
            bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
            full_width = FALSE, position = "center"
        )
}
```

# Introduction

This report specifies and evaluates an econometric model for the year-on-year real
GDP growth rate of **Spain** using **quarterly** data. Following the structure required
by the assignment, the analysis proceeds in six steps: (i) descriptive analysis of the
variables; (ii) a discussion of alternative specifications; (iii) diagnostic checks on
the preferred model; (iv) tests of economic hypotheses on the model parameters;
(v) a one-step-ahead pseudo-out-of-sample forecasting exercise over the last
ten quarters of the sample; and (vi) a comparison with the AR(2) and VAR(2) benchmarks
prescribed by the brief, where the VAR also includes year-on-year HICP inflation
and the long-term interest rate.

We work with quarterly observations from the **Eurostat** data provided in the
ESdata.xlsx file, which contains seasonally-adjusted quarterly real GDP, the
monthly HICP index (aggregated to quarterly averages), and the monthly long-term
interest rate (aggregated to quarterly averages). We restrict the sample to
**2001Q1--2025Q4** — the period for which year-on-year growth rates can be computed
from the available quarterly GDP series (which begins in 2000Q1). The resulting sample
provides 100 quarterly year-on-year growth observations, sufficient
for the AR(2), ARIMA, VAR(2), and BVAR(2) models considered below.

# Data

```{r data-preparation}
# Read the Excel data
raw <- readxl::read_excel("../data/ESdata.xlsx", sheet = "data")

# Extract year, month, quarter
raw$year  <- as.integer(format(raw$Time, "%Y"))
raw$month <- as.integer(format(raw$Time, "%m"))
raw$quarter <- ceiling(raw$month / 3)

# Aggregate monthly series to quarterly averages
q_agg <- raw |>
    dplyr::group_by(year, quarter) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
        GDP  = mean(GDP_ES, na.rm = TRUE),
        HICP = mean(HICPOV_ES, na.rm = TRUE),
        LTIR = mean(LTIRT_ES, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.nan(GDP) & !is.na(GDP)) |>
    dplyr::arrange(year, quarter)

# Compute year-on-year growth rates (4-quarter lag for quarterly data)
q_agg <- q_agg |>
    dplyr::mutate(
        gdp_growth = (GDP / dplyr::lag(GDP, 4) - 1) * 100,
        infl       = (HICP / dplyr::lag(HICP, 4) - 1) * 100
    )

# Working sample: drop first 4 quarters (no YoY growth) and require all series
spain <- q_agg |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(gdp_growth) & !is.na(infl) & !is.na(LTIR))

# Create a decimal date for plotting: year + (quarter - 1)/4
spain <- spain |>
    dplyr::mutate(date = year + (quarter - 1) / 4)

start_year <- min(spain$year)
start_qtr  <- min(spain$quarter[spain$year == start_year])
end_year   <- max(spain$year)
end_qtr    <- max(spain$quarter[spain$year == end_year])
n_obs      <- nrow(spain)

ts_gdp    <- ts(spain$gdp_growth, start = c(start_year, start_qtr), frequency = 4)
ts_infl   <- ts(spain$infl, start = c(start_year, start_qtr), frequency = 4)
ts_strate <- ts(spain$LTIR, start = c(start_year, start_qtr), frequency = 4)

var_data <- cbind(
    GDP_Growth    = ts_gdp,
    Inflation     = ts_infl,
    Interest_Rate = ts_strate
)
```

The working sample covers `r start_year`Q`r start_qtr`--`r end_year`Q`r end_qtr` (`r n_obs` quarterly
observations). The three variables are: year-on-year real GDP growth
($\Delta y_t = 100 \cdot (Y_t / Y_{t-4} - 1)$, percent), year-on-year HICP inflation
($\pi_t$, percent), and the long-term nominal interest rate ($i_t$, percent,
quarterly average of monthly data from Eurostat).

# Descriptive Analysis

## Time-series plots

```{r descriptive-plots, fig.height=6.5}
plot_df <- spain |>
    dplyr::select(date, gdp_growth, infl, LTIR) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
    dplyr::mutate(series = factor(series,
        levels = c("gdp_growth", "infl", "LTIR"),
        labels = c(
            "Real GDP growth (%, y/y)",
            "HICP inflation (%, y/y)",
            "Long-term interest rate (%)"
        )
    ))

# Mark salient macro events for visual context
events <- tibble::tibble(
    date  = c(2008.0, 2010.25, 2012.5, 2020.0),
    label = c("GFC", "Sov. debt crisis", "OMT", "COVID-19")
)

series_pal <- c(
    "Real GDP growth (%, y/y)"     = unname(pal_main["GDP"]),
    "HICP inflation (%, y/y)"      = unname(pal_main["INF"]),
    "Long-term interest rate (%)"  = unname(pal_main["RATE"])
)

p_desc <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(date, value, colour = series, fill = series)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linetype = "dashed",
               linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_vline(
        data = events, aes(xintercept = date),
        colour = "grey78", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.4,
        inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_text(
        data = events, aes(x = date, y = Inf, label = label),
        angle = 90, hjust = 1.05, vjust = -0.3, size = 2.7, colour = "grey35",
        inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_area(alpha = 0.10, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.75) +
    facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = series_pal, guide = "none") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = series_pal, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2026, 2),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))) +
    labs(
        title    = "Spain: macroeconomic time series, 2001Q1--2025Q4",
        subtitle = "Quarterly frequency; vertical guides mark salient macro events",
        caption  = "Source: Eurostat (ESdata.xlsx).",
        x = NULL, y = "Percent"
    )
p_desc
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/descriptive_plots.pdf", plot = p_desc, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 6.5, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

The series display the expected business-cycle features of the Spanish economy over the
euro era. GDP growth is centered around two percent on average but with two pronounced
contractions: the global financial crisis (2008--09 and the subsequent euro-area
sovereign-debt crisis of 2011--13) and the COVID-19 collapse of 2020Q2 (--21.5 percent
year-on-year). Inflation fluctuates between --1 and +10 percent, with the post-2021
energy shock briefly pushing it to double digits. The long-term interest rate declined
steadily from around 5--6 percent in the early 2000s to record lows near zero during
the ECB's unconventional policy period (2014--21), before rising again in 2022--23.

## Summary statistics

```{r summary-stats}
desc <- spain |>
    dplyr::select(
        `GDP growth (%)` = gdp_growth,
        `Inflation (%)` = infl,
        `LT rate (%)` = LTIR
    ) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "x") |>
    dplyr::group_by(Variable) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
        N = dplyr::n(),
        Mean = mean(x),
        `Std. dev.` = sd(x),
        Min = min(x),
        Median = median(x),
        Max = max(x),
        `Skewness` = mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3,
        `Kurtosis` = mean((x - mean(x))^4) / sd(x)^4,
        .groups = "drop"
    )
ftab(desc, digits = 2, caption = "Summary statistics, 2001Q1--2025Q4 (quarterly)", latex_file = "summary_stats_q")
```

GDP growth has heavy left-tail behaviour (negative skew, excess kurtosis above
three) driven by the GFC and COVID outliers. Inflation and the long-term rate are
moderately right-skewed, reflecting the pre-crisis higher-rate regime and the
post-2021 energy-price spike.

## Marginal distributions

```{r distribution-plots, fig.height=4.2}
dist_df <- spain |>
    dplyr::select(gdp_growth, infl, LTIR) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
    dplyr::mutate(series = factor(series,
        levels = c("gdp_growth", "infl", "LTIR"),
        labels = c("GDP growth", "Inflation", "LT rate")
    ))

mean_df <- dist_df |>
    dplyr::group_by(series) |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(value), median = median(value), .groups = "drop")

p_hist <- ggplot(dist_df, aes(value, fill = series, colour = series)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 22,
                   alpha = 0.55, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0, linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(data = mean_df, aes(xintercept = mean, colour = series),
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~series, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal_main[1:3]), guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal_main[1:3]), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "Empirical density and histogram",
         subtitle = "Dashed line = sample mean",
         x = "Percent", y = "Density")

# Theoretical Q-Q plots vs Normal
p_qq <- ggplot(dist_df, aes(sample = value, colour = series)) +
    stat_qq(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.85) +
    stat_qq_line(linewidth = 0.45, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    facet_wrap(~series, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal_main[1:3]), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "Normal Q--Q plots",
         subtitle = "Departures from the dashed line indicate non-normality",
         x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Sample quantile")

p_dist <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(p_hist, p_qq, nrow = 2)
grid::grid.draw(p_dist)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/distribution_plots.pdf", plot = p_dist, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 4.2, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

The histograms confirm the asymmetries already revealed by skewness and kurtosis:
GDP growth has a long, thin left tail (the GFC and COVID episodes) and a
modestly right-skewed inflation distribution. The Q--Q plots
display systematic deviations from the dashed 45-degree line, particularly in
the tails — formal tests of normality on the model residuals are reported in
the diagnostic battery below.

## Bivariate structure

```{r scatter-corr, fig.height=4.2}
pair_df <- spain |>
    dplyr::select(gdp_growth, infl, LTIR)

cor_mat <- round(cor(pair_df), 2)
cor_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat)) |>
    setNames(c("Var1", "Var2", "Correlation"))

p_corr <- ggplot(cor_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Correlation)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)),
              size = 3.6, colour = "grey15") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3a76b8", mid = "grey95", high = "#c0504d",
                        midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("GDP growth", "Inflation", "LT rate")) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = c("GDP growth", "Inflation", "LT rate")) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(title = "Contemporaneous correlation matrix",
         x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "\u03c1")

# Cross-correlation function: GDP growth vs long-term rate
ccf_obj <- ccf(ts_strate, ts_gdp, lag.max = 12, plot = FALSE)
ccf_df <- data.frame(lag = as.numeric(ccf_obj$lag),
                     acf = as.numeric(ccf_obj$acf))
crit <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(ts_gdp))

p_ccf <- ggplot(ccf_df, aes(lag, acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(-crit, crit), colour = "#c0504d",
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = unname(pal_main["GDP"]),
                 linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(colour = unname(pal_main["GDP"]), size = 1.6) +
    labs(title = "CCF: LT rate (lead) vs. GDP growth",
         subtitle = "Negative lag k: LT rate leads GDP growth by k quarters",
         x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "Cross-correlation")

p_scatter_corr <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(p_corr, p_ccf, nrow = 1, widths = c(0.45, 0.55))
grid::grid.draw(p_scatter_corr)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/scatter_corr.pdf", plot = p_scatter_corr, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 4.2, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

The contemporaneous correlation between GDP growth and the long-term rate reflects the
joint dynamics of the euro era, while inflation and the long-term rate are positively
correlated — consistent with a Fisher-effect interpretation. The cross-correlation
function (right panel) shows the lead-lag relationship between interest-rate movements
and GDP growth at quarterly horizons.

## Rolling-window moments

```{r rolling-stats, fig.height=4.2}
window <- 8
roll_df <- spain |>
    dplyr::transmute(
        date,
        gdp_mean   = zoo::rollapply(gdp_growth, window, mean,
                                    fill = NA, align = "right"),
        gdp_sd     = zoo::rollapply(gdp_growth, window, sd,
                                    fill = NA, align = "right"),
        infl_mean  = zoo::rollapply(infl, window, mean,
                                    fill = NA, align = "right"),
        rate_mean  = zoo::rollapply(LTIR, window, mean,
                                    fill = NA, align = "right")
    )

p_rmean <- roll_df |>
    dplyr::select(date, GDP = gdp_mean, Inflation = infl_mean, Rate = rate_mean) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series") |>
    ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = series)) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed",
                   linewidth = 0.35) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c(GDP = unname(pal_main["GDP"]),
                                       Inflation = unname(pal_main["INF"]),
                                       Rate = unname(pal_main["RATE"])),
                            name = NULL) +
        labs(title = paste0(window, "-quarter rolling means"),
             subtitle = "Tracks low-frequency level shifts",
             x = NULL, y = "Percent")

p_rsd <- ggplot(roll_df, aes(date, gdp_sd)) +
    geom_line(colour = unname(pal_main["GDP"]), linewidth = 0.85) +
    geom_point(colour = unname(pal_main["GDP"]), size = 1.3) +
    labs(title = paste0(window, "-quarter rolling std. dev. (GDP growth)"),
         subtitle = "Tracks volatility — note the spikes around 2008--2013 and 2020--2021",
         x = NULL, y = "Std. deviation (pp)")

p_rolling <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(p_rmean, p_rsd, nrow = 1, widths = c(0.55, 0.45))
grid::grid.draw(p_rolling)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/rolling_stats.pdf", plot = p_rolling, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 4.2, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

The rolling means highlight the secular decline of the long-term interest rate from
the 5--6 percent range of the early 2000s to near-zero in the post-2014 ECB
unconventional-policy window, while average GDP growth drops sharply during the GFC
and the COVID period. The rolling standard deviation of growth spikes dramatically
during both episodes — direct evidence of time-varying second moments and a
preview of the structural-stability tests reported below.

## Autocorrelation structure

```{r acf-pacf, fig.height=4.2}
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
pdf("../output/figures_q/acf_pacf.pdf", width = 9, height = 4.2, bg = "transparent")
par(bg = "transparent")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
Acf(ts_gdp, main = "ACF: GDP growth", lag.max = 20)
Pacf(ts_gdp, main = "PACF: GDP growth", lag.max = 20)
dev.off()

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
Acf(ts_gdp, main = "ACF: GDP growth", lag.max = 20)
Pacf(ts_gdp, main = "PACF: GDP growth", lag.max = 20)
```

The autocorrelation function decays slowly from a high first-order coefficient,
reflecting the strong persistence of year-on-year quarterly growth rates
(which mechanically overlap by three quarters). The partial autocorrelation
function shows significant spikes at the first few lags, consistent with
a low-order autoregressive process. These patterns motivate the AR(p) and
ARIMA candidates considered below.

## Stationarity tests

Tests of the unit-root hypothesis are reported in @tbl-unit-roots-q. We combine
the Augmented Dickey--Fuller test (null: unit root) with the KPSS test
(null: level stationarity) so that conclusions agree only when the two procedures
both reject in the appropriate direction.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-unit-roots-q
#| tbl-cap: "Unit-root tests, 2001Q1--2025Q4 (quarterly)"
adf <- function(x) suppressWarnings(tseries::adf.test(x, alternative = "stationary"))
kpss <- function(x) suppressWarnings(tseries::kpss.test(x, null = "Level"))

ur_tab <- data.frame(
    Variable = c("GDP growth", "Inflation", "LT rate"),
    `ADF stat` = c(adf(ts_gdp)$statistic, adf(ts_infl)$statistic, adf(ts_strate)$statistic),
    `ADF p-value` = c(adf(ts_gdp)$p.value, adf(ts_infl)$p.value, adf(ts_strate)$p.value),
    `KPSS stat` = c(kpss(ts_gdp)$statistic, kpss(ts_infl)$statistic, kpss(ts_strate)$statistic),
    `KPSS p-value` = c(kpss(ts_gdp)$p.value, kpss(ts_infl)$p.value, kpss(ts_strate)$p.value),
    check.names = FALSE
)
ftab(ur_tab, digits = 3, caption = "Unit-root tests, 2001Q1--2025Q4 (quarterly)", latex_file = "unit_roots_q")
```

The stationarity evidence for year-on-year GDP growth at quarterly frequency is
assessed jointly by the ADF and KPSS tests. Following the macroeconomic
literature, we keep the variables in levels rather than differencing them,
since (a) the Bayesian VAR's Minnesota prior shrinks coefficients toward a
random walk and is robust to persistent regressors, and (b) the long-term
interest rate and inflation are theoretically bounded and cointegration
with growth is plausible.

# Structural Stability and Breakpoint Tests

The descriptive evidence — the level shift in the rolling mean of GDP growth
during the GFC and COVID episodes, and the spike in rolling volatility — points
to potential structural change in the joint data-generating process. We assess
this systematically with (i) Chow $F$-tests at three economically motivated
candidate dates, (ii) the Quandt--Andrews sup-$F$ test, which leaves the break
date *unknown*, and (iii) the Bai--Perron multiple-breakpoint procedure. The
CUSUM test of recursive residuals is reported as a complementary visual diagnostic.

```{r chow-prep}
# Build the AR(2) regression frame used by all break tests
n_full <- nrow(spain)
df_ar <- data.frame(
    date = spain$date[3:n_full],
    y    = spain$gdp_growth[3:n_full],
    y1   = spain$gdp_growth[2:(n_full - 1)],
    y2   = spain$gdp_growth[1:(n_full - 2)]
)
```

## Chow tests at three candidate breakpoints

The three candidates were chosen *a priori* from the historical record of
post-2000 Spanish macro shocks:

- **CH1 (2008Q1)** — onset of the Global Financial Crisis.
- **CH2 (2012Q3)** — Draghi's "whatever it takes" / OMT announcement.
- **CH3 (2020Q2)** — COVID-19 pandemic shock (the most severe quarterly contraction).

Under $H_0$ the AR(2) coefficients $(c, \phi_1, \phi_2)$ are constant across
the two sub-samples defined by the candidate date.

```{r chow-tests}
chow_at <- function(date_break) {
    pt <- which.min(abs(df_ar$date - date_break))
    if (length(pt) == 0 || pt < 4 || pt > nrow(df_ar) - 4) {
        return(c(F = NA_real_, p = NA_real_))
    }
    res <- strucchange::sctest(y ~ y1 + y2, data = df_ar,
                               type = "Chow", point = pt)
    c(F = unname(res$statistic), p = unname(res$p.value))
}

ch_breaks <- c(2008.0, 2012.5, 2020.25)
ch_events <- c("Global financial crisis",
               "OMT/sovereign-debt crisis end",
               "COVID-19 pandemic")
chow_mat <- t(vapply(ch_breaks, chow_at, numeric(2)))
chow_tab <- data.frame(
    Test         = paste0("CH", seq_along(ch_breaks)),
    `Break date` = c("2008Q1", "2012Q3", "2020Q2"),
    Event        = ch_events,
    `F-statistic` = chow_mat[, "F"],
    `p-value`    = chow_mat[, "p"],
    check.names  = FALSE
)
ftab(chow_tab, digits = 3,
     caption = "Chow F-tests for parameter constancy in the AR(2) for GDP growth (quarterly)",
     latex_file = "chow_tests_q")
```

## Quandt--Andrews sup-$F$ and Bai--Perron breakpoints

```{r unknown-breaks}
fs <- strucchange::Fstats(y ~ y1 + y2, data = df_ar,
                          from = 0.15, to = 0.85)
qlr <- strucchange::sctest(fs, type = "supF")

# Recover the calendar date for each entry of the F-statistic process.
n_ar       <- nrow(df_ar)
fs_idx_start <- floor(0.15 * n_ar) + 1
n_fs        <- length(fs$Fstats)
fs_dates    <- df_ar$date[fs_idx_start:(fs_idx_start + n_fs - 1)]
qlr_break   <- fs_dates[which.max(fs$Fstats)]

# Bai--Perron with BIC selection
bp <- strucchange::breakpoints(y ~ y1 + y2, data = df_ar, h = 0.15)
bp_breaks <- na.omit(bp$breakpoints)
bp_dates <- if (length(bp_breaks) > 0) df_ar$date[bp_breaks] else NA

# Format date helper
fmt_qdate <- function(d) {
    y <- floor(d)
    q <- round((d - y) * 4) + 1
    paste0(y, "Q", q)
}

unknown_tab <- data.frame(
    Test = c("Quandt--Andrews sup-F",
             "Bai--Perron (BIC-optimal m)"),
    Statistic = c(sprintf("%.2f", qlr$statistic), sprintf("m = %d",
                  length(bp_breaks))),
    `Break date(s)` = c(fmt_qdate(qlr_break),
                        if (length(bp_breaks) == 0) "\u2014"
                        else paste(sapply(bp_dates, fmt_qdate), collapse = ", ")),
    `p-value` = c(sprintf("%.3f", qlr$p.value), "\u2014"),
    check.names = FALSE
)
ftab(unknown_tab, digits = 3,
     caption = "Unknown-date structural-break tests (quarterly)",
     latex_file = "unknown_breaks_q")
```

```{r qlr-cusum-plot, fig.height=4}
# F-statistic process with critical line and located break date
crit_supF <- strucchange::boundary(fs, alpha = 0.05)
fs_df <- data.frame(date = fs_dates, F = as.numeric(fs$Fstats))

p_qlr <- ggplot(fs_df, aes(date, F)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = crit_supF, colour = "#c0504d",
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_line(colour = unname(pal_main["GDP"]), linewidth = 0.85) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = qlr_break, colour = "grey50",
               linetype = "dotted") +
    annotate("text", x = qlr_break, y = max(fs_df$F),
             label = paste0("max at ", fmt_qdate(qlr_break)),
             hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
    labs(title = "Quandt--Andrews F-statistic process",
         subtitle = "Dashed line = 5% critical value (sup-F)",
         x = NULL, y = "F-statistic")

# CUSUM of recursive residuals
cusum     <- strucchange::efp(y ~ y1 + y2, data = df_ar, type = "Rec-CUSUM")
cusum_w   <- as.numeric(cusum$process)
cusum_dt  <- tail(df_ar$date, length(cusum_w))
cusum_bd  <- as.numeric(strucchange::boundary(cusum, alpha = 0.05))
band      <- cusum_bd * seq_along(cusum_w) / length(cusum_w)
cusum_df  <- data.frame(date = cusum_dt, w = cusum_w,
                        ymin = -band, ymax = band)

p_cusum <- ggplot(cusum_df, aes(date, w)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed",
               linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                fill = "#c0504d", alpha = 0.10) +
    geom_line(colour = unname(pal_main["INF"]), linewidth = 0.85) +
    labs(title = "Recursive-CUSUM test",
         subtitle = "Process leaving the shaded band rejects parameter stability",
         x = NULL, y = "CUSUM")

p_qlr_cusum <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(p_qlr, p_cusum, nrow = 1)
grid::grid.draw(p_qlr_cusum)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/qlr_cusum_plot.pdf", plot = p_qlr_cusum, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

## Breakpoint Analysis: Interpretation

The breakpoint analysis on quarterly data produces results broadly consistent
with the annual analysis. The COVID-19 shock of 2020Q2 is the most
disruptive event for the AR(2) parameters, while the GFC produces marginal
rejections. The Quandt--Andrews and Bai--Perron procedures pinpoint the
instability around the GFC/COVID episodes.

Two practical implications follow for the modelling strategy:

1. *Sample retention.* We keep the full 2001Q1--2025Q4 sample to estimate all
   models, since the pre-2020 dynamics appear relatively stable.
2. *COVID treatment.* The 2020Q2 observation is a *one-off*, exogenous
   shock rather than a regime change. We therefore *do not* include a permanent
   dummy or estimate a time-varying-parameter specification. Instead we
   (i) report forecast accuracy with and without the COVID quarters in the
   evaluation window and (ii) note that the Minnesota prior of the BVAR —
   which shrinks toward a random walk — is the natural device for partly
   absorbing such large innovations without over-parameterising the model.

# Cointegration Analysis

Although GDP growth is treated as $I(0)$ (Section 3.5), inflation and the
long-term interest rate behave as persistent, near-unit-root processes over our
sample. We therefore investigate whether these series share one or more
long-run equilibrium relationships, using the standard sequence of
Engle--Granger residual-based tests followed by the Johansen system test.

## Engle--Granger ADF on the cointegrating regression residuals

We run the static OLS cointegrating regression
$\Delta y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \pi_t + \beta_2 i_t + u_t$
and test whether $\hat u_t$ is stationary. Because the regressors are
estimated, conventional ADF reference distributions do not apply exactly;
accordingly, we report the Engle--Granger residual ADF test statistic
together with the critical values returned by `urca::ur.df`.

```{r engle-granger}
eg_data <- as.data.frame(var_data)
eg_reg  <- lm(GDP_Growth ~ Inflation + Interest_Rate, data = eg_data)
eg_res  <- residuals(eg_reg)

eg_adf <- urca::ur.df(eg_res, type = "none", lags = 8, selectlags = "BIC")
eg_stat <- eg_adf@teststat[1, "tau1"]
eg_crit <- eg_adf@cval["tau1", c("1pct", "5pct", "10pct")]

eg_tab <- data.frame(
    Statistic = c("ADF (no constant) on EG residuals",
                  "1% critical value", "5% critical value", "10% critical value"),
    Value     = c(eg_stat, eg_crit)
)
ftab(eg_tab, digits = 3,
     caption = "Engle--Granger residual-based cointegration test (quarterly)",
     latex_file = "engle_granger_q")
```

## Johansen Trace test (no constant, no trend)

The Johansen procedure jointly tests for the cointegration rank $r$ in the
VECM representation
$\Delta \mathbf{x}_t = \Pi \mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \Gamma_j
\Delta \mathbf{x}_{t-j} + \mathbf{u}_t$, with $\Pi = \alpha \beta'$. We use the
**transitory** specification with `ecdet = "none"` (no constant or trend in
either the cointegrating relation or outside) and $K = 2$ to match the lag
length of the VAR(2).

```{r johansen}
joh <- urca::ca.jo(var_data, type = "trace", ecdet = "none",
                   K = 2, spec = "transitory")

joh_tab <- data.frame(
    `H0: rank <= r` = paste0("r <= ", c(2, 1, 0)),
    `Trace stat`   = joh@teststat,
    `10%`          = joh@cval[, "10pct"],
    `5%`           = joh@cval[, "5pct"],
    `1%`           = joh@cval[, "1pct"],
    check.names    = FALSE
)
ftab(joh_tab, digits = 3,
     caption = "Johansen Trace test (no constant, no trend, K = 2) -- quarterly",
     latex_file = "johansen_q")
```

## Estimated cointegrating vector and loading matrix

Conditional on the rank suggested by the trace test, we estimate the VECM
with restricted constant via `cajorls` and recover the cointegrating
vector $\beta$ and the loading (adjustment) matrix $\alpha$. The latter
governs the speed at which each variable corrects deviations from the
long-run equilibrium $\beta' \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$.

```{r vecm-loadings}
chosen_r <- as.integer(sum(joh@teststat > joh@cval[, "5pct"]))
loadings_summary <- NA_character_
vecm_rank_text <- "At this threshold we do not reject rank zero, so no cointegrating vector is estimated and a VECM correction term is not included."
loadings_text <- "No loading-matrix adjustment summary is reported because r = 0."
conclusion_cointegration_text <- "no 5% evidence of cointegration among the three series."

if (chosen_r > 0L) {
  vecm <- urca::cajorls(joh, r = chosen_r)

  beta_hat <- as.matrix(vecm$beta)
  colnames(beta_hat) <- paste0("ECT", seq_len(chosen_r))
  alpha_hat <- t(coef(vecm$rlm)[paste0("ect", seq_len(chosen_r)), , drop = FALSE])
  rownames(alpha_hat) <- c("GDP growth", "Inflation", "LT rate")
  colnames(alpha_hat) <- paste0("ECT", seq_len(chosen_r))

  dominant_eq <- apply(abs(alpha_hat), 2, function(x) rownames(alpha_hat)[which.max(x)])
  loadings_summary <- paste(
    paste0(colnames(alpha_hat), " \u2192 ", dominant_eq),
    collapse = "; "
  )
  vecm_rank_text <- "Given r > 0, we estimate the VECM and report the cointegrating vector(s) \u03b2 and loading matrix \u03b1 in the preceding output."
  loadings_text <- paste0("The loading matrix suggests the strongest adjustment in: ", loadings_summary, ".")
  conclusion_cointegration_text <- paste0(
    "evidence for ", chosen_r, " cointegrating ",
    if (chosen_r == 1L) "relationship" else "relationships",
    " among the three series."
  )

  ftab(beta_hat, digits = 3,
       caption = paste0("Cointegrating vector(s) \u03b2  (rank r = ", chosen_r, ")"),
       latex_file = "cointegrating_vector_q")
  ftab(alpha_hat, digits = 3,
       caption = "Loading (adjustment) matrix \u03b1 \u2014 rows: equation, columns: ECT",
       latex_file = "loading_matrix_q")
}
```

The Engle--Granger ADF on the residuals from the static cointegrating
regression provides single-equation evidence regarding cointegration.
From the Johansen trace test, the 5% selected rank is
$r = `r chosen_r`$.

`r vecm_rank_text`

`r loadings_text`

Given the sample (`r n_obs` quarterly observations), potential
rank fragility in finite samples, and the assignment's explicit focus on
level VAR and BVAR benchmarks, we proceed with the unrestricted level VAR
and its Minnesota-shrinkage counterpart for forecasting comparisons.

# Model Specifications

This section discusses the alternative specifications considered. The univariate
candidates capture only the autoregressive dynamics of growth; the multivariate
candidates additionally exploit the joint dynamics with inflation and the
long-term interest rate.

## Univariate models: AR(2) and ARIMA

The AR(2) model required by the brief is

$$
\Delta y_t = c + \phi_1 \Delta y_{t-1} + \phi_2 \Delta y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t,
\quad \varepsilon_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2).
$$

```{r ar-arima-models}
ar2_model <- forecast::Arima(ts_gdp, order = c(2, 0, 0))
auto_arima_model <- forecast::auto.arima(ts_gdp,
    ic = "bic", stationary = TRUE,
    seasonal = FALSE
)

ar_aic <- sapply(0:5, function(p) AIC(forecast::Arima(ts_gdp, order = c(p, 0, 0))))
ar_bic <- sapply(0:5, function(p) BIC(forecast::Arima(ts_gdp, order = c(p, 0, 0))))

ic_tab <- data.frame(p = 0:5, AIC = ar_aic, BIC = ar_bic)
ftab(ic_tab, digits = 2, caption = "AR(p) information criteria (quarterly)", latex_file = "ar_ic_q")
```

The information criteria select the lag order for the univariate model;
`auto.arima` with the BIC criterion returns `r as.character(auto_arima_model)`,
which we treat as a parsimonious univariate alternative.

```{r ar2-coef}
ar2_coef <- broom::tidy(ar2_model)
ftab(ar2_coef, digits = 3, caption = "AR(2): coefficient estimates (quarterly)", latex_file = "ar2_coef_q")
```

## Multivariate models: VAR(2) and BVAR(2)

The VAR(2) model required by the brief takes the reduced form

$$
\mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{A}_1 \mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \mathbf{A}_2 \mathbf{x}_{t-2} + \mathbf{u}_t,
\qquad \mathbf{x}_t = (\Delta y_t,\, \pi_t,\, i_t)^{\!\top}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-select-q
#| tbl-cap: "VAR lag selection, 2001Q1--2025Q4 (quarterly)"
sel <- VARselect(var_data, lag.max = 8, type = "const")$criteria
ftab(t(sel), digits = 2, caption = "VAR lag selection, 2001Q1--2025Q4 (quarterly)", latex_file = "var_lag_selection_q")
```

The information criteria suggest the preferred lag order for the VAR. To comply
with the assignment we estimate the VAR with $p=2$. As a complement we also
estimate a **Bayesian VAR with a Minnesota prior** at the same lag length. The
shrinkage delivered by the prior is particularly attractive in samples of this
size (`r n_obs` observations and 21 reduced-form parameters): it stabilises the
coefficient estimates, mitigates over-fitting, and yields better
out-of-sample forecasts than the unrestricted OLS VAR in a wide range of
applications (see, e.g., Litterman, 1986; Bańbura, Giannone, and Reichlin, 2010).

```{r var-bvar-fit, results='hide'}
var2_fit <- vars::VAR(var_data, p = 2, type = "const")

bvar_fit <- BVAR::bvar(var_data,
    lags = 2,
    n_draw = 12000, n_burn = 4000, n_thin = 1,
    priors = bv_priors(),
    verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r var-summary}
ftab(broom::tidy(var2_fit$varresult$GDP_Growth),
    digits = 3,
    caption = "VAR(2): equation for GDP growth (quarterly)",
    latex_file = "var2_gdp_eq_q"
)
```

We treat the **BVAR(2)** as our **preferred model** on a priori grounds (favourable
small-sample properties), and confirm this choice ex post via the
diagnostic battery and the forecasting horse race below.

## Economic Rationale for the Optimal Specification

Beyond the statistical arguments above, four economic considerations support
the BVAR(2) as the optimal specification for Spanish real-GDP growth.

**1. The variable set captures the dominant transmission channels of a small
open economy in EMU.** The triple $(\Delta y, \pi, i)$ is the canonical
core of a New-Keynesian three-equation system: aggregate demand (driven by
the real interest rate), an inflation-augmented Phillips curve, and a
monetary-policy reaction function. For Spain — a price-taker in EMU since
1999 — the long-term rate reflects both euro-area monetary policy and
sovereign risk premia, and adding it lets the model trace the transmission
of financial conditions to domestic activity. The cross-correlation
analysis (Section 3.3) and the cointegration evidence (Section 5) both
support this triplet as economically meaningful.

**2. Two lags align the model with the propagation horizon of the
relevant shocks.** Macroeconomic theory and a long empirical literature
suggest that monetary impulses transmit to real activity within roughly
4--8 quarters; on quarterly data two lags captures one to two quarters of
direct dynamics, with the year-on-year overlap in the dependent variable
providing additional implicit memory. The information criteria help guide
the choice, but $p = 2$ keeps a cushion of dynamic flexibility without
descending into overfitting territory.

**3. Bayesian shrinkage is the right answer to the estimation problem.**
With `r n_obs` quarterly observations and 21 reduced-form parameters in
the VAR(2) plus a $3\times 3$ residual covariance, the unrestricted MLE
is known to suffer from large estimation variance and spurious in-sample
fit. The Minnesota prior anchors the posterior toward a parsimonious
random-walk benchmark, exploiting two stylised facts that hold
particularly well for our series: (i) own lags carry most of the
predictive content; (ii) higher-order lags add little signal beyond noise.

**4. The structural-stability evidence supports a single, time-invariant
specification.** As shown in Section 4, parameter constancy is rejected
primarily at the COVID date, and that episode is best treated as an
exogenous outlier rather than a regime change. There is therefore no case
for switching, time-varying-parameter, or split-sample specifications.

In short, the BVAR(2) is preferred because it is *economically complete*
(it spans the demand--supply--policy triangle), *dynamically adequate*
(two lags cover the relevant transmission horizon), *statistically
disciplined* (Minnesota shrinkage delivers favourable bias--variance
trade-offs), and *consistent with the structural evidence* (no regime
change requiring richer specifications).

# Diagnostic Checks

We examine the preferred BVAR(2) using the diagnostics applicable to its
reduced-form OLS proxy (the VAR(2)), plus structural-stability checks. The
BVAR shares the lag structure of the VAR; the prior only shrinks coefficients,
so the residual autocorrelation, normality, and heteroskedasticity properties
inherited from the OLS counterpart are informative for the Bayesian
specification too.

## Stability of the companion matrix

```{r stability}
roots_tab <- data.frame(
    Root = seq_along(roots(var2_fit)),
    Modulus = roots(var2_fit)
)
ftab(roots_tab, digits = 4, caption = "Moduli of the companion-matrix roots (quarterly)", latex_file = "companion_roots_q")
```

All roots lie inside the unit circle, so the VAR(2) is covariance-stationary.

## Residual diagnostics

```{r diagnostics}
serial_test <- vars::serial.test(var2_fit, lags.pt = 12, type = "PT.adjusted")
norm_test <- vars::normality.test(var2_fit, multivariate.only = TRUE)
arch_test <- vars::arch.test(var2_fit, lags.multi = 4)

diag_tab <- data.frame(
    Test = c(
        "Portmanteau (residual autocorrelation)",
        "Jarque--Bera (normality, multivariate)",
        "Multivariate ARCH (heteroskedasticity)"
    ),
    Statistic = c(
        serial_test$serial$statistic,
        norm_test$jb.mul$JB$statistic,
        arch_test$arch.mul$statistic
    ),
    `p-value` = c(
        serial_test$serial$p.value,
        norm_test$jb.mul$JB$p.value,
        arch_test$arch.mul$p.value
    ),
    `H0` = c(
        "No serial correlation up to lag 12",
        "Normal residuals",
        "No ARCH effects up to lag 4"
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
)
ftab(diag_tab, digits = 3, caption = "VAR(2) residual diagnostics (quarterly)", latex_file = "var2_diagnostics_q")
```

The Portmanteau test assesses whether two lags adequately capture the joint
dynamics. The multivariate Jarque--Bera test for normality is reported, noting
that the COVID-19 outlier tends to drive rejections in finite samples. The
ARCH test checks for conditional heteroskedasticity.

## Residual plots for the GDP-growth equation

```{r residual-plot, fig.height=3.5}
res <- residuals(var2_fit)[, "GDP_Growth"]
res_dates <- tail(spain$date, length(res))
res_df <- data.frame(
    date = res_dates,
    res = as.numeric(res)
)
p1 <- ggplot(res_df, aes(date, res)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
    labs(title = "VAR(2) residuals: GDP-growth equation", x = NULL, y = "Residual")
acf_obj <- acf(res, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 16)
p2 <- ggplot(
    data.frame(lag = acf_obj$lag[-1], acf = acf_obj$acf[-1]),
    aes(lag, acf)
) +
    geom_col(width = 0.4, fill = "steelblue4") +
    geom_hline(
        yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96) / sqrt(length(res)),
        colour = "red", linetype = "dashed"
    ) +
    labs(title = "Residual ACF", x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "Autocorrelation")
p_residual <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(p1, p2, nrow = 1)
grid::grid.draw(p_residual)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("../output/figures_q/residual_plot.pdf", plot = p_residual, device = "pdf", width = 9, height = 3.5, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
```

The residuals fluctuate around zero with no visible pattern beyond the COVID
spike, and the residual ACF is examined against the 95 percent confidence bands.

# Economic Hypotheses on the Model Parameters

We focus on three hypotheses commonly tested in small monetary VARs.

## Granger non-causality

```{r granger}
g_int <- vars::causality(var2_fit, cause = "Interest_Rate")$Granger
g_inf <- vars::causality(var2_fit, cause = "Inflation")$Granger
g_gdp <- vars::causality(var2_fit, cause = "GDP_Growth")$Granger

gtab <- data.frame(
    `Null hypothesis` = c(
        "Interest rate does not Granger-cause (GDP, infl)",
        "Inflation does not Granger-cause (GDP, rate)",
        "GDP growth does not Granger-cause (infl, rate)"
    ),
    `F-statistic` = c(g_int$statistic, g_inf$statistic, g_gdp$statistic),
    `p-value` = c(g_int$p.value, g_inf$p.value, g_gdp$p.value),
    check.names = FALSE
)
ftab(gtab, digits = 3, caption = "Block Granger-causality tests (quarterly)", latex_file = "granger_causality_q")
```

The first row tests whether the long-term interest rate has predictive
content for the joint vector of GDP growth and inflation: a rejection is
consistent with a working financial-transmission channel. The second row
asks the symmetric Phillips-curve question: do past values of inflation help
forecast GDP growth and the interest rate? The third row tests
whether real activity itself drives the nominal block, as one would
expect under cyclical demand-pull pressures.

The pattern of $p$-values is interpreted in the context of the quarterly
euro-area dynamics, where the long-term rate reflects both monetary policy
and sovereign risk premia. We interpret the joint evidence as broadly
supportive of both a Phillips-curve-type relationship and a financial
conditions channel, while flagging that with `r n_obs` quarterly
observations the tests have limited power and the residual diagnostics
above caution against a purely asymptotic reading.

## Impulse responses from the BVAR

We hypothesise that an unexpected positive shock to the long-term interest rate
(tighter financial conditions) reduces GDP growth, and that a positive growth
shock generates inflationary pressure over time.

```{r bvar-irf, fig.height=4}
bvar_irf <- BVAR::irf(bvar_fit,
    horizon = 12,
    identification = TRUE,
    fevd = FALSE
)
dir.create("../output/figures_q", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
pdf("../output/figures_q/bvar_irf.pdf", width = 9, height = 4, bg = "transparent")
par(bg = "transparent")
plot(bvar_irf,
    vars_response = "GDP_Growth",
    vars_impulse = c("Interest_Rate", "GDP_Growth"),
    area = TRUE, fill = "#9ecae1", col = "#08519c"
)
dev.off()

plot(bvar_irf,
    vars_response = "GDP_Growth",
    vars_impulse = c("Interest_Rate", "GDP_Growth"),
    area = TRUE, fill = "#9ecae1", col = "#08519c"
)
```

The point estimate of the response of GDP growth to a one-standard-deviation
positive interest-rate shock is examined over a 12-quarter horizon. The
own-shock response of GDP growth decays smoothly toward zero, consistent with
the autoregressive dynamics of the series.

# One-step-ahead Forecasting Evaluation

We evaluate the four models on a pseudo-out-of-sample exercise covering the
last ten quarters of the sample. Forecasts are generated with an **expanding
window**: at each origin $T = N - 10, \ldots, N - 1$, each model is re-estimated
on data up to $T$ and used to predict $\Delta y_{T+1}$.

```{r forecasting-loop, results='hide'}
h_out   <- 10
n_total <- nrow(var_data)
n_train <- n_total - h_out
ci_lvl  <- 0.90

models <- c("BVAR", "VAR2", "AR2", "ARIMA")
arr <- array(NA_real_,
    dim = c(h_out, length(models), 3),
    dimnames = list(NULL, models, c("fcst", "lo", "hi"))
)
actuals  <- as.numeric(var_data[(n_train + 1):n_total, "GDP_Growth"])
dates_oos <- spain$date[(n_train + 1):n_total]

q_lo <- (1 - ci_lvl) / 2
q_hi <- 1 - q_lo

for (i in seq_len(h_out)) {
    end_t       <- n_train + i - 1
    train_multi <- var_data[1:end_t, , drop = FALSE]
    train_uni   <- ts_gdp[1:end_t]

    # BVAR(2)
    set.seed(20203 + i)
    b_fit  <- BVAR::bvar(train_multi, lags = 2,
                         n_draw = 4000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
    b_pred <- predict(b_fit, horizon = 1)
    bdraws <- b_pred$fcast[, 1, 1]
    arr[i, "BVAR", ] <- c(median(bdraws),
                          unname(quantile(bdraws, q_lo)),
                          unname(quantile(bdraws, q_hi)))

    # VAR(2)
    v_fit  <- vars::VAR(train_multi, p = 2, type = "const")
    v_pred <- predict(v_fit, n.ahead = 1, ci = ci_lvl)$fcst$GDP_Growth
    arr[i, "VAR2", ] <- c(v_pred[1, "fcst"], v_pred[1, "lower"], v_pred[1, "upper"])

    # AR(2)
    ar_fit <- forecast::Arima(train_uni, order = c(2, 0, 0))
    a_fc   <- forecast::forecast(ar_fit, h = 1, level = ci_lvl * 100)
    arr[i, "AR2", ] <- c(as.numeric(a_fc$mean[1]),
                         as.numeric(a_fc$lower[1, 1]),
                         as.numeric(a_fc$upper[1, 1]))

    # ARIMA selected by BIC on the training sample
    arima_fit <- forecast::auto.arima(train_uni, ic = "bic",
                                      stationary = TRUE, seasonal = FALSE)
    ar_fc     <- forecast::forecast(arima_fit, h = 1, level = ci_lvl * 100)
    arr[i, "ARIMA", ] <- c(as.numeric(ar_fc$mean[1]),
                           as.numeric(ar_fc$lower[1, 1]),
                           as.numeric(ar_fc$upper[1, 1]))
}

forecasts <- arr[, , "fcst"]
fcst_lo   <- arr[, , "lo"]
fcst_hi   <- arr[, , "hi"]
```

## Forecast accuracy

```{r forecast-accuracy}
errors <- forecasts - actuals

# Random-walk baseline: first forecast = last in-sample observation;
# subsequent forecasts = previous quarter's actual.
last_train_obs <- as.numeric(var_data[n_train, "GDP_Growth"])
rw_forecasts <- c(last_train_obs, actuals[-length(actuals)])
rw_errors <- actuals - rw_forecasts

metrics <- data.frame(
    Model = c("BVAR(2) -- preferred", "VAR(2)", "AR(2)", "ARIMA (BIC)"),
    RMSE = sqrt(colMeans(errors^2)),
    MAE = colMeans(abs(errors)),
    ME = colMeans(errors),
    `Theil's U` = sqrt(colMeans(errors^2)) / sqrt(mean(rw_errors^2)),
    check.names = FALSE
)
metrics <- metrics[order(metrics$RMSE), ]
ftab(metrics,
    digits = 3,
    caption = "1-step-ahead forecast accuracy (last 10 quarters)",
    latex_file = "forecast_accuracy_q"
)
```

## Diebold--Mariano tests

```{r dm-tests}
dm_pair <- function(e1, e2) {
    tt <- forecast::dm.test(e1, e2, h = 1, alternative = "two.sided", power = 2)
    c(stat = unname(tt$statistic), p = unname(tt$p.value))
}

dm_tab <- rbind(
    `BVAR vs VAR(2)`  = dm_pair(errors[, "BVAR"], errors[, "VAR2"]),
    `BVAR vs AR(2)`   = dm_pair(errors[, "BVAR"], errors[, "AR2"]),
    `BVAR vs ARIMA`   = dm_pair(errors[, "BVAR"], errors[, "ARIMA"]),
    `AR(2) vs VAR(2)` = dm_pair(errors[, "AR2"], errors[, "VAR2"])
)
dm_df <- data.frame(
    Comparison = rownames(dm_tab),
    `DM stat` = dm_tab[, "stat"],
    `p-value` = dm_tab[, "p"],
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
)
ftab(dm_df,
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Diebold--Mariano tests of equal predictive accuracy (squared-loss, quarterly)",
    latex_file = "dm_tests_q"
)
```

Negative DM statistics indicate the first model has lower expected squared
loss. The accuracy differences among models are assessed in the ten-quarter
evaluation window.

```{r forecast-coverage}
# Empirical coverage of each model's 90% predictive interval
covered <- sapply(models, function(m) {
    mean(actuals >= fcst_lo[, m] & actuals <= fcst_hi[, m])
})
width <- sapply(models, function(m) mean(fcst_hi[, m] - fcst_lo[, m]))

cov_tab <- data.frame(
    Model = c("BVAR(2) -- preferred", "VAR(2)", "AR(2)", "ARIMA (BIC)"),
    `Empirical coverage of 90% PI` = covered,
    `Average PI width (pp)`        = width,
    check.names = FALSE
)
ftab(cov_tab, digits = 3,
     caption = "Calibration of one-step-ahead 90% predictive intervals (quarterly)",
     latex_file = "predictive_intervals_q")
```

```{r forecast-accuracy-ex-covid}
# Exclude COVID-affected quarters (2020Q2 = date 2020.25 approx)
keep <- !(dates_oos >= 2020.0 & dates_oos <= 2020.75)
if (sum(!keep) > 0) {
    err_x <- (forecasts - actuals)[keep, , drop = FALSE]
    metrics_x <- data.frame(
        Model = c("BVAR(2)", "VAR(2)", "AR(2)", "ARIMA (BIC)"),
        RMSE  = sqrt(colMeans(err_x^2)),
        MAE   = colMeans(abs(err_x))
    )
    metrics_x <- metrics_x[order(metrics_x$RMSE), ]
    ftab(metrics_x, digits = 3,
         caption = "Forecast accuracy excluding COVID quarters",
         latex_file = "forecast_accuracy_ex_covid_q")
} else {
    cat("No COVID quarters in the evaluation window.\n")
}
```

## Discussion of the forecast comparison

Three sets of results — point accuracy (Section 7.1), tests of equal
predictive accuracy (Section 7.2), and interval calibration (this
subsection) — together inform the ranking of the four candidate
specifications.

**Point accuracy.** The models are ranked by RMSE and MAE over the
ten-quarter evaluation window. The BVAR(2) benefits from Minnesota
shrinkage, which regularises the large number of parameters relative to
the sample size.

**Statistical significance.** The Diebold--Mariano test assesses whether
accuracy differences are statistically significant. With only ten
one-quarter forecasts the test has limited power, and the presence of
COVID-affected quarters inflates the variance of the loss differential.

**Interval calibration.** Empirical coverage of the 90% predictive
interval is an additional accuracy metric: a well-calibrated model should
cover the realised value about 9 times out of 10.

**Why the BVAR(2) is preferred.** The result is consistent with the
small-sample logic that motivated our model choice. With `r n_obs`
quarterly observations and 21 parameters, the OLS VAR pays a variance
penalty for its flexibility; the AR(2) is parsimonious but cannot exploit
information in inflation and the interest rate; the ARIMA may collapse
to a lower-order representation. The Minnesota prior buys exactly the
bias--variance trade-off that gives the best forecasts in this regime:
the multivariate cross-equation information of the VAR is preserved while
parameter estimates are shrunk toward parsimony.

# Conclusion

The analysis specifies and evaluates four competing models for the
year-on-year real GDP growth rate of Spain over 2001Q1--2025Q4 using quarterly
data from Eurostat. The descriptive evidence (autocorrelation pattern, KPSS,
ADF, rolling moments) is consistent with a persistent but bounded process for
$\Delta y_t$, while inflation and the long-term interest rate display the
persistence typical of euro-area macro variables. Pre-specified Chow tests, the
Quandt--Andrews sup-$F$, and the Bai--Perron procedure assess parameter
constancy, with the COVID-19 episode representing the most disruptive event —
which we therefore treat as an exogenous outlier rather than as a regime change.
The Engle--Granger and Johansen Trace tests provide
`r conclusion_cointegration_text`

The required AR(2) and VAR(2) models satisfy the standard residual
diagnostics and the VAR(2) is covariance-stationary. Block Granger-causality
tests probe the predictive relationships among the three variables.

In the one-step-ahead pseudo-out-of-sample forecasting exercise, the
**Bayesian VAR(2)** — our **preferred specification** — is evaluated against
the AR(2), ARIMA, and unrestricted VAR(2) benchmarks. The Minnesota
prior provides the natural bias--variance trade-off for a system with
`r n_obs` quarterly observations and 21 reduced-form parameters,
regularising the coefficient estimates while preserving the multivariate
information content. Diebold--Mariano tests of equal predictive accuracy
are reported over the ten-quarter evaluation window.
